sentences.text: Back at the palafito, they moved quickly.
Isla checked on Abuelo — his fever was worse.
His breathing was shallow.
He mumbled something Isla did not understand, and then he was quiet.
She put a fresh cool cloth on his forehead.
She kissed his hand.
She went back to the kitchen.
Camila had already put water on the stove.
Isla read Abuela's recipe out loud, twice, to make sure she had it right.
Two handfuls of the leaves, chopped fine.
Half a liter of water.
Boil for exactly the length of the song, no more, no less — the song they had sung in the forest.
Then strain.
Then add one small pinch of sea salt.
That was for the body.
Give in small warm sips, every hour, for four hours.
If the fever breaks, stop giving.
If it does not break, come back in the morning and go get more plants.
They chopped the leaves.
They put them in the boiling water.
Camila sang the song again, three times, to time the boil — Isla checked with the clock, and the song lasted almost exactly three minutes each time, so they let it boil for three songs.
Camila's voice was steady and calm.
It was a strange thing to hear in the kitchen — this small old song, in a language neither of them fully spoke, being used as a timer for their grandfather's medicine.
Isla strained the tea into a small ceramic cup.
She added the pinch of sea salt.
She smelled it.
It smelled green, like the forest.
She carried it into Abuelo's room.
Camila followed with a small spoon and a folded towel.
Isla sat down on the edge of the bed.
She lifted Abuelo's head a little, and she brought the spoon of tea to his mouth, and she said, softly, "Abuelo.
Please.
It is us.
Drink a little."
He drank.
Slowly, but he drank.
Sometimes he opened his eyes and looked at Isla, and sometimes he closed them and just swallowed.
She gave him small sips every ten minutes for the first hour.
Then every fifteen minutes.
Then every half hour.
Camila brought fresh cool cloths.
Isla read to Abuelo, quietly, from a book of stories that had been Abuela's — even though she was not sure if he was really listening — because she thought maybe her voice would help.
She had heard once that people who were very sick could still hear voices.
At about eight o'clock in the evening, Abuelo opened his eyes.
He looked at Isla.
He said, in a very tired voice, "Nietita." Little granddaughter.
And Isla started to cry.
She was so tired she had not known she was going to cry.
She just did.
Abuelo lifted his hand — slowly, unsteadily — and put it on hers.
He was still hot.
But he was there.
He was talking.
"You made me tea," he said.
"Yes," said Isla.
"Camila and I did." Abuelo said, "Your Abuela — she taught you." Isla said, "She wrote it down.
In her book.
We found it."
In the morning, Abuelo's fever had broken.
Isla could tell before she even touched him because he was breathing normally, deeply, the way people breathe when they are truly asleep.
She put her hand on his forehead.
He was cool.
He was properly cool.
She sat down on the floor beside his bed and she cried a little more, quietly, so she would not wake him.
Then she went back to the kitchen.
Camila was already up.
Camila was sitting at the kitchen table with the notebook open in front of her, looking at a page.
"Is he better," Camila said, without looking up.
"He is better," said Isla.
"His fever is gone." Camila nodded.
She kept looking at the notebook.
She said, "I want to learn more songs." Isla sat down next to her.
She looked over Camila's shoulder.
The page Camila was on had a plant called peumo — a note said it was for children's coughs.
Isla could read that Camila had already learned that one before Abuela died.
She said, "Yes.
We will learn more songs." And Camila nodded again, and turned the page.
The ferry came at ten.
The doctor from Achao — a small serious man with a black bag — walked up from the pier with Isla and Camila.
Abuelo was sitting up in bed by then, tired but talking.
The doctor looked him over.
He listened to his chest.
He took his temperature.
He asked Isla what she had given him.
Isla told him.
She showed him the notebook.
The doctor read the page.
He looked at the pressed leaf.
He was quiet for a long time.
Then he looked at Isla and Camila.
He said, "You two saved his life.
Do you understand that?
If he had not had that tea, he would have gotten worse in the night.
He might not have made it until the ferry." Isla did not know what to say.
She had not been thinking about it that way.
She had only been thinking that Abuelo was sick and there was a book and they had to try.
She said, quietly, "Our Abuela was a meica.
She taught us." The doctor nodded slowly.
"Yes," he said.
"She did.
Keep that book somewhere safe.
Someday you will teach it to someone else." And he looked at Isla, and at Camila, and he did not have to say who.
That was in the autumn.
By the winter, Abuelo was fully himself again.
And every Saturday, from then on, Isla and Camila took the notebook and they walked into the forest, and Camila sang, and Isla wrote.
Not for anyone else.
Just because.
Because someone had to.
